History and Physical (H&P – Detailed)

Consult Summary:
26-year-old female primary-school teacher presents with a 3-day history of new-onset dry, itchy, red rash on both hands and arms beginning after swimming; no systemic symptoms; impression is dermatitis treated conservatively with topical steroids, emollients, and OTC antihistamines.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Dry, itchy skin (hands and arms).  
• Onset/progression: Started “a few days ago”; temporal association with swimming session; persistent despite self-applied coconut butter.  
• Character: Redness and pruritus; denies spots/pustules, fever, sweating, skin discharge, or cracking.  
• Exacerbating factors: None identified; patient attributes possible weather influence; work-related stress noted.  
• Relieving factors tried: Coconut butter (no benefit).  
• Associated review of systems:  
  – Constitutional: Feels tired; no fever, appetite intact.  
  – GI/GU: No vomiting, no diarrhea, normal bowel and urinary habits.  
  – No cardiorespiratory or neurologic complaints reported.  
• Pertinent negatives: No prior similar episodes; no eczema or chronic skin disease history.

Past Medical History:
• No chronic medical conditions reported.  
• No past dermatologic conditions.

Medications:
• Microgynon (combined oral contraceptive) – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• No other current medications.  

Allergies:
• Possible lactose intolerance (food). No drug or environmental allergies reported.

Social History:
• Lives alone.  
• Occupation: Primary-school teacher; currently under increased work stress and long hours.  
• Non-smoker, minimal alcohol, denies recreational drug use.

Family History:
• Father – asthma.  
• Mother – hay fever.  
• No known familial skin disorders.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: Not recorded.  
• Skin and general examination: Not performed/documented during virtual consult.

Investigations:
• None ordered at this visit.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
Likely irritant/contact dermatitis of hands and forearms post-swimming; no red-flag features or systemic involvement.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Contact/irritant dermatitis (most likely) – onset after swimming exposure to chlorine; localized erythematous pruritic rash; supports physician impression.  
2. Atopic dermatitis – personal history negative but family atopy (asthma, hay fever) present; stress can exacerbate; lacks chronicity (opposing evidence).  
3. Xerotic eczema due to dry/cold weather – patient suspects weather; generalized dryness possible; less clear temporal trigger.

Issue 1: Dermatitis (probable contact/irritant)
• Provide patient information leaflet on dermatitis.  
• Start medium-potency topical steroid cream (name/strength not specified).  
• Liberal use of emollients throughout the day for hydration.  
• Consider OTC oral antihistamines (e.g., chlorpheniramine, loratadine) for pruritus.  
• Advise to avoid further swimming/exposure to potential irritants until resolution.  
• Re-evaluate in 1 week if no improvement or earlier if worsening/secondary infection develops.

Issue 2: Work-related stress / fatigue
• Acknowledge stress; encourage routine stress-management strategies (sleep hygiene, breaks).  
• No specific referral requested; monitor at follow-up.

Issue 3: Health maintenance / contraception
• Continue Microgynon as prescribed; no concerns raised.  
• Reminded patient of regular reviews for contraceptive use (blood pressure, etc.) – not done today due to virtual format.

General plan items:
• Safety-net advice given: seek care sooner for spreading rash, pain, swelling, fever, or skin discharge.  
• Follow-up: virtual or in-person review next week if symptoms persist.

Quality checks:
● Vitals and objective skin examination not documented (virtual consult limitation).  
● Exact steroid preparation, strength, dose, and frequency not specified.  
● Medication and allergy reconciliation limited; no drug allergies explicitly confirmed.  
● No DDx dataset available; differential constructed from transcript only.  
● Transcript clear; minor conversational gaps but clinical content adequate.
